articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document serves as the masthead for "EPHEMERIS," the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It identifies the issue as Volume 2, Number 2, published in February 1990, indicating a regular newsletter from an astronomy club.

articles.title: FIELD OF VIEW
articles.summary: This month's events feature a talk by Joe Wujek of the Lowell Observatory Advisory Board on Percival Lowell, Martian Canals, and an Arizona Observatory, preceded by annual elections for the Board of Directors. Additional activities include a public star party on February 2nd, a monthly Board Meeting on February 10th, and two more star parties on February 17th and 24th.

articles.title: ELECTIONS
articles.summary: The February meeting is designated as the Annual Meeting where the Board of Directors is elected. Five members will continue their terms, while four candidates are up for election or reelection to the board. Following the board elections, officers will be chosen from the newly formed board at the February 10th meeting.

articles.title: PHOTOGRAPHER AT LARGE
articles.summary: The article expresses gratitude to Robert Keller for his excellent photography featured in recent issues of the Ephemeris. He is frequently present at General Meetings and Astronomy Classes, capturing club activities, and members are encouraged to be camera-ready.

articles.title: BRANHAM LANE STAR PARTIES
articles.summary: The SJAA is hosting a series of public star parties on various Fridays throughout the year, from February to December. Attendees are encouraged to bring their telescopes and invite friends, with contact information for Tom Ahl or Jim Van Nuland available for further details.

articles.title: FEBRUARY STARRY NIGHTS
articles.summary: This article outlines astronomical events and observing opportunities for February, including the minor Delta Leonids meteor shower and detailed Galilean satellite events for Jupiter observers on February 17th. It also presents NGC 2685 (the Helix Galaxy) as a deep-sky challenge and discusses moon-related superstitions, alongside a comprehensive list of club meetings and public star parties for February and early March.

articles.title: PART ONE: NEWTONIAN NUGGETS
articles.summary: The author, a visual observer, shares his journey into the 'eternal collimation' of his reflecting telescopes, driven by a desire for optical perfection and an absorbing hobby. After initial struggles with rudimentary methods, he acquired a Tectron Collimator kit, which ultimately helped him diagnose a faulty diagonal mirror and achieve significantly improved optical alignment. This pursuit transformed his observing experience, leading to clearer views of celestial objects.

articles.title: THE CELESTIAL TOURIST SPEAKS
articles.summary: This article delves into the common debate among amateur astronomers concerning telescope objectives, specifically the interplay between aperture size and optical quality. The author proposes two complementary rules: "Aperture is not substitute for optical quality" and "Optical quality is no substitute for aperture," explaining that these address the distinct goals of observing fine detail versus faint objects. He illustrates the significant advantage of larger aperture for light gathering and viewing deep-sky objects by comparing his 90mm refractor, 8-inch Dobsonian, and 14-inch Celestron telescopes.

articles.title: SPACE PROGRAM UPDATE
articles.summary: This article delves into the various factors, beyond just aperture, that significantly limit a telescope's performance, particularly regarding resolving power and contrast. It details how optical quality, specific design elements like spider arms and secondary mirror obstruction, and manufacturing difficulties (especially with aspheric optics in larger amateur telescopes) diminish image fidelity. The author emphasizes that these challenges often mean larger, more affordable amateur telescopes may not achieve their full theoretical potential due to inherent optical compromises.

articles.title: PLANNED EVENTS IN THE U.S. 1990 SPACE PROGRAM
articles.summary: The document outlines the planned U.S. space program events for 1990, detailing several Space Shuttle launches and their respective payloads. Key missions include the deployment of the Hubble Space Telescope, the Gamma Ray Observatory, the Astro-1 spacelab, and a Galileo spacecraft flyby of Venus, alongside classified military payloads.

articles.title: STAA EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document, titled "STAA Ephemeris," lists a series of significant space-related events with their corresponding dates. It details various spacecraft arrivals and launches, including the Magellan Spacecraft at Venus, several Space Shuttle missions (Columbia, Atlantis, Discovery) carrying scientific laboratories and probes, and the Galileo spacecraft's first Earth flyby.

articles.title: PLANNED EUROPEAN ARIANE LAUNCH SCHEDULE FOR 1990
articles.summary: This document outlines the planned European Ariane launch schedule for 1990, detailing monthly missions throughout the year. It lists a variety of satellites from different nations, including remote sensing, telecommunication, meteorological, and Earth resource spacecraft. The schedule indicates a busy year for European space launches, serving both European and international clients.

articles.title: FIRST COMMERCIAL TITAN FLIGHT LAUNCHED NEW YEAR'S EVE
articles.summary: Martin Marietta successfully launched its first commercial Titan flight on New Year's Eve, deploying two communication satellites and becoming the second company to enter the commercial launch market. This follows McDonnell Douglas's inaugural commercial launch last August, with General Dynamics also set to join the market soon. Martin Marietta has already secured three more customers for future Titan launches.

articles.title: JAPANESE SPACE PROGRAM INCLUDES LUNAR MISSIONS
articles.summary: Japan's space program plans to launch a dual satellite, Muses-A, to the Moon on January 23, 1990. This mission aims to gain experience in determining spacecraft orbits around a planetary body and to demonstrate high-efficiency data transmission technology crucial for future lunar and Venus missions. Japan also seeks to contribute to the U.S. lunar base initiative.

articles.title: SOVIETS REVEAL 1960'S MANNED MOON PLANS
articles.summary: The Soviets recently revealed details and hardware of their 1960s manned Moon landing program to U.S. aerospace engineers. Their plan involved sending two cosmonauts to the Moon, with one landing on the surface, using the N1 heavy-lift booster similar to the U.S. Saturn 5. The program was ultimately halted due to four test failures of the N1 booster.

articles.title: SOVIETS EXPANDING THE MIR SPACE STATION
articles.summary: The Soviet Union is expanding its Mir space station with four new modules. The first, Kvant-2 (Module D), which includes a Manned Maneuvering Unit, docked on December 6th. Upcoming modules include Module T for semiconductor production, Module O with an optical payload, and an ecological platform designed for international use.

articles.title: DOUBLE, TRIPLE & MULTIPLE STARS
articles.summary: Patrick M. Donnelly provides an observing guide for numerous double, triple, and multiple stars in the constellation Perseus, a challenging target when high overhead in early February. The guide details specific star systems such as Zeta, Epsilon, Mu, Theta, Tau, and Eta Persei, providing observational data like magnitudes, separations, and position angles, along with recommendations for telescope sizes. It also highlights interesting doubles within the M34 open cluster and briefly mentions a search for a faint component of Lambda Orionis.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: Don Machholz's "COMET COMMENTS" provides an update on recent cometary activity, detailing the discovery of three new comets: Comet Austin (1989c1), Periodic Comet Skorichenko-George (1989e1), and Comet McKenzie-Russell (1989f1), along with their discovery circumstances and future visibility. It also reports on the status of other comets, including the recovery of Periodic Comet Van Biesbroeck and the ongoing observation of Tuttle-Giacobini-Kresak, while noting the fading of others.

articles.title: OFFICERS AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors for an organization. It details various leadership positions, including President, Vice President, Treasurer, Secretary, and Editor, along with several Directors. Contact phone numbers are provided for most individuals listed in these roles.

articles.title: COMET EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document provides detailed ephemeris data for two comets, Periodic Comet Tuttle-Giacobini-Kresak (1989k) and Comet Skorichenko-George (1989e), for late January through early March. The tables list celestial coordinates (RA and DEC for J1950 and J2000 epochs), elongation, sky visibility, and estimated visual magnitude to aid observers in locating these objects.

articles.title: JUPITER'S RED SPOT
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for observing Jupiter's Great Red Spot (GRS). It lists specific dates and times in February and early March when the GRS will be transiting the meridian as viewed from the Pacific Standard Time (PST) zone, aiding observers in planning their viewing sessions.

articles.title: GREAT RED SPOT
articles.summary: This article provides observing tips for Jupiter's Great Red Spot (GRS), noting that it is now high enough for observation. It highlights that even small telescopes, like an 80mm refractor, can reveal the GRS and other details, encouraging observers to sketch their findings. The author also reports on the continued absence of the South Equatorial Belt (SEB) and offers advice on optimal viewing conditions and techniques for spotting the GRS.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: This document features a series of free, non-commercial classified advertisements for astronomically related products and services. It primarily lists various telescopes such as Celestron and Meade models, along with optical accessories like finders, eyepieces, filters, and other equipment like tripods and cold cameras. Instructions for submitting ads to the editor are also provided.

articles.title: THE STORY OF A TELESCOPE IN MEXICO
articles.summary: Rick McWilliams recounts his adventurous trip to Los Barilles, Baja California Sur, Mexico, bringing his bulky 20-inch Dobsonian telescope. He faced significant challenges with Mexican customs regarding its temporary importation but eventually succeeded in setting it up for impromptu star parties, sharing views of celestial objects with amazed locals and tourists. Despite the logistical hurdles, the experience underscored the joy of sharing amateur astronomy.

articles.title: ALMOST A STAR
articles.summary: Jupiter, primarily composed of hydrogen and helium, is a gaseous planet that radiates internal heat from its formation, maintaining a constant temperature. The article explains that Jupiter is near the maximum size for a planet, and if it were approximately 60 times more massive, thermonuclear reactions would ignite, causing it to become a self-luminous star.

articles.title: JUPITER'S CORE
articles.summary: Jupiter's deep interior core is likely composed of iron and silicates, roughly the size of Earth or Venus. It boasts an extreme temperature of about 30,000 degrees Celsius and experiences immense pressure, more than 30 million times that of Earth's atmosphere. These conditions are sufficient to compress a planet like Earth to less than half its diameter.

articles.title: THE JOVIAN SEA
articles.summary: Jupiter's interior features a massive shell of metallic hydrogen, an exotic form not found on Earth, spanning over 25,000 miles around its core under immense pressure and high temperatures. Outside this, a 15,000-mile-thick layer of liquid hydrogen forms what can be considered Jupiter's "surface," existing at extremely low temperatures before transitioning into the gaseous atmosphere and cloud layers.

articles.title: THE JOVIAN CLOUDS
articles.summary: Jupiter's atmosphere is characterized by distinct cloud layers, including high white and yellow ammonia crystal clouds, a lower layer of ammonium hydrosulfide crystals, and the deepest layer composed of water droplets and ice crystals. While the lowest water cloud layer exhibits Earth-like temperatures, the overall atmosphere remains unbreathable due to its composition of hydrogen, helium, and noxious gases like ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, phosgene, and cyanide, lacking essential oxygen.

articles.title: THE GREAT RED SPOT
articles.summary: The Great Red Spot on Jupiter is a massive, enduring storm that has been raging for over 300 years. This cyclonic system is incredibly vast, reaching a diameter of up to 25,000 miles, making it three times the size of Earth and the largest known storm in the solar system.

articles.title: SPIN, JUPITER, SPIN
articles.summary: Jupiter holds the title as the solar system's fastest rotating planet, completing a spin every 10 hours at its equator, resulting in an impressive speed of 27,720 mph (44,601 km/h). This equatorial speed significantly surpasses Earth's escape velocity, and the article notes it took Voyager 1 approximately 1,300 Jupiter spins to reach the giant planet after its 1977 launch.

articles.title: SIZING UP THE GIANT
articles.summary: The article describes Jupiter as the largest planet in our solar system, containing 71 percent of the total planetary mass. It emphasizes Jupiter's immense size, noting its diameter is 11 times that of Earth and using vivid analogies to illustrate its significantly larger surface area compared to our home planet.

articles.title: A SATURN V LAUNCHED FROM JUPITER
articles.summary: Jupiter, possessing the solar system's highest escape velocity due to its immense gravity, would pose an insurmountable challenge for a Saturn V rocket. If launched from Jupiter's liquid hydrogen surface, the rocket would struggle to gain speed, burning through its first stage with minimal range before the second stage would ignite but ultimately crash, performing no better than a long-range artillery shell.

articles.title: THE FASTEST MOON
articles.summary: Designated 1979 J3 and discovered by the Voyager spacecraft, this small moon holds the record as the fastest-moving moon in our solar system. It orbits Jupiter in just over 7 hours, covering an average distance of 35,000 miles at an incredible speed of 70,400 miles per hour.

articles.title: SAN JOSE ASTRONOMICAL ASSOCIATION MEMBERSHIP APPLICATION
articles.summary: This document is a membership application for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), detailing different membership types like 'Membership Only', 'Membership/S&T', and 'Junior' along with their respective fees. It provides instructions for submitting the application, contact information for the treasurer, and details about the association's monthly publication, 'EPHEMERIS', including submission guidelines for members.
